claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is ductile and contains an FCC matrix with B2 precipitates.
The as-cast alloy has no significant L12 ordering.
The as-cast alloy has relatively smooth phase boundaries that permit cross-slip and high ductility.
Aging near 600°C produces a high density of near-stoichiometric Ni3Al L12-ordered domains in the FCC matrix.
The brittle window begins when L12 ordering reaches a critical threshold.
Increasing the degree of L12 ordering raises the antiphase boundary energy.
Aging near 600°C produces jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries whose serrations concentrate stress.
High APBE combined with jagged B2/FCC boundaries inhibits dislocation cross-slip.
Restricted cross-slip forces planar slip, causing localized stress accumulation and brittle fracture.
Aging near 750°C decreases the L12 order parameter.
The reduction in L12 order at 750°C lowers APBE.
Aging near 750°C makes the phase boundaries less jagged or creates ductile transition zones along them.
Reduced ordering and modified boundaries at 750°C restore cross-slip and ductility.
Ductility varies non-monotonically with aging temperature and reaches a minimum near 600°C.
Nanoindentation will show greater local hardness at jagged B2/FCC interfaces after aging at 600°C than after aging at 750°C.
Nanoindentation will show a lower pop-in load at the jagged interfaces in the 600°C-aged state, indicating more restricted dislocation nucleation or motion.
TEM of the brittle 600°C-aged state will reveal a high density of planar slip bands and sharp, jagged interfaces.
TEM of the ductile 750°C-aged state will reveal wavy slip and smoother interfaces.
The critical ordering and boundary-roughness condition is typically reached in the 550–650°C aging regime.
The relevant chemical-ordering threshold is near the stoichiometric Ni3Al condition, although no numerical order parameter is specified.

contradictions.description: The mechanism asserts restricted dislocation nucleation or motion at the 600°C interfaces, but the predicted decrease in pop-in load ordinarily denotes easier onset of a discrete plastic event. The proposed interpretation of lower pop-in load is therefore internally inconsistent unless an alternative pop-in mechanism is specified.
